enrichment.short_title: MOD employee manual handling injury appeal dismissed
key_facts: Mrs Bennetts, a 64-year-old MOD civilian worker at Yeovilton, injured her back on 25 July 2000 while trying to lift a mail sack onto a trolley to decant stuck contents.
Her normal procedure was to sort post on the floor; the injury occurred when the sack caught on the trolley and she tugged against its weight.
The recorder found no breach of regulation 4 because decanting mail bags did not pose a real risk in normal handling, and any post-accident assessment risks were not causally linked.
The recorder also found 60 per cent contributory negligence if liability had arisen.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court judgment dismissing a personal injury claim brought in negligence and under the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no breach of statutory duty or common law negligence established on causation grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Even if a post-injury manual handling assessment indicated medium risk from stooping in normal procedures, that risk was not relevant to the mechanism of this one-off injury caused by the sack snagging on a trolley; the employer's duties under regulation 4 did not extend to preventing an untrained employee's novel and unusual lifting manoeuvre where training would not have altered the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether decanting mail sacks involved a real risk triggering regulation 4 duties
Meaning of risk under regulation 4 compared with common law negligence
Causation between any breach and the injury mechanism
Whether negligent packing of mail bags caused the injury
Contributory negligence

enrichment.short_title: No implied duty to protect employee's economic welfare
key_facts: Mr Crossley, a senior director of Faithful & Gould, went on sick leave in December 1996 with depression and sought early retirement on health grounds.
While employed he had a contractual right to long-term disability benefits under a group insurance scheme; on termination benefits became discretionary.
The employer knew resignation would end his as-of-right entitlement but did not warn him when assisting with retirement letters for tax efficiency.
UNUM paid benefits until June 1998 but not thereafter after his employment ended.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court decision dismissing claims for breach of implied contractual terms relating to pension and disability scheme benefits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no implied portmanteau obligation to take reasonable care for economic well-being and Scally criteria not satisfied.
enrichment.ratio: There is no general implied term in contracts of employment requiring employers to take reasonable care for employees' economic welfare; even where an employer knows resignation will prejudice disability scheme benefits, no duty arises to warn a senior employee who could reasonably be expected to understand the scheme or obtain advice from his pensions broker.
legal_issues: Whether a general implied term protects employees' economic well-being
Employer's duty when requesting resignation letters affecting insurance benefits
Application of Scally criteria to senior employees with access to advice
Distinction between Hedley Byrne advice duties and general financial protection

enrichment.short_title: Intra-group property transfer as trading stock for tax
key_facts: New Angel Court Ltd, a Hilton Group property dealer, acquired nine commercial properties from fellow group companies on 13 November 1996.
The vendor companies held the properties as capital investments, not trading stock; the properties were pregnant with about £68M capital losses.
NAC sold most properties at a profit and claimed a trading loss on acquisition enabling group relief; the Revenue disputed trading stock characterisation.
Special Commissioners and Lawrence Collins J held the transfers were not acquisitions as trading stock; the Court of Appeal reversed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from Special Commissioners and High Court on whether intra-group property acquisitions qualified as trading stock under section 173(1) TCGA 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; properties acquired as trading stock; Special Commissioners and judge erred in treating group disposal policy as negativing trading purpose.
enrichment.ratio: Fiscal motive does not prevent an asset being acquired as trading stock under section 173(1) where the asset is of a kind sold in the company's ordinary course and acquired for trading with a view to resale at profit; group purpose to dispose of investment properties cannot negative the trading purpose identifiable when NAC in isolation bought and sold at market prices for real profit.

enrichment.short_title: Tipstaff assault on McKenzie friend in family proceedings
key_facts: Dr Pelling acted as McKenzie friend for a father in long-running residence proceedings; Singer J ordered a 10-year-old boy to stay with his mother for two days.

Leveson J found trivial intentional physical contact constituting assault but rejected misfeasance and Article 8 claims.

enrichment.short_title: Disability living allowance mobility component permission refused

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mr McKee, a disabled retired miner, received disability living allowance including the higher mobility component based on walking no more than 30–50 yards before dyspnoea.

enrichment.short_title: Partition deed vehicular right of way over flagged path
key_facts: The Wray at Grasmere was divided into two dwellings by a 1971 Deed of Partition between the Brooks and Griffiths families.
No 2 owners claimed a vehicular right of way across the front of No 1 wider than the existing slate path; the Georges cross-appealed for footpath-only access.
The judge had held vehicular access limited to 6 feet 6 inches straddling the path; neither party supported that width on appeal.
The flagged path laid in 1969 was about three feet wide and the front gates about eight feet six inches.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from county court construction of easement rights in a 1971 Deed of Partition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and cross-appeal allowed; vehicular right confined to the flagged path, not a wider car route across the front garden.
enrichment.ratio: A grant of right of way with or without vehicles over passageways edged brown identifies existing passageways first and only permits vehicles that fit on them; it is improbable the parties intended a small road in front of French windows when a carport existed and the obvious passageway was the slate path.
legal_issues: Construction of express vehicular easement in a partition deed
Whether passageways include grass strips beside a flagged path
Relevance of carport and improbability of front vehicular access
Effect of conveyancing rule allowing grantee to improve access

enrichment.short_title: Court Service employee remitted for constructive dismissal findings
key_facts: Wendy Comfort, a Court Service HEO, sought appointment as Newport County Court manager after Cardiff and Swansea court groups merged.
She was offered training and shadowing but resigned in April 2001 claiming constructive dismissal, disability discrimination, and redundancy.
The tribunal found disability but no discrimination and rejected constructive dismissal; a sharp dispute arose over what Mr Risk said at September and October 2000 meetings.
Metadata on Mr Risk's meeting notes suggested they were typed in January 2001, not contemporaneously, but the tribunal made no findings on authenticity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissing appeal against Employment Tribunal rejection of constructive dismissal and redundancy claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; ET and EAT decisions on constructive dismissal and redundancy set aside; remitted to a differently constituted tribunal with expedition.
enrichment.ratio: An employment tribunal commits an error of law if it decides constructive dismissal without resolving an important disputed fact—what a senior manager said at meetings central to the claim—including whether allegedly contemporaneous notes were authentic; such disputes cannot be treated as immaterial or otiose without explanation.

enrichment.short_title: VAT recovery assessments time-barred after Primback
key_facts: DFS accounted for VAT on full customer prices on interest-free credit sales but received lower sums from finance companies.
Following the Court of Appeal decision in Primback, DFS received about £13.1M repayments and £1.5M interest in 1996–97.
After the ECJ judgment in Primback in May 2001 the Commissioners issued recovery assessments; DFS argued they were out of time under section 78A(2).
The tribunal held the ECJ judgment was evidence of law not fact; the Vice-Chancellor allowed the Commissioners' appeal; the Court of Appeal restored the tribunal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal on preliminary issue whether VAT recovery assessments under sections 80(4A) and 78A were made within the section 78A(2) limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; assessments out of time; ECJ judgment legal effect is not evidence of facts for section 78A(2) purposes.
enrichment.ratio: The legal effect of a judicial decision is not a fact within the natural meaning of evidence of facts in section 78A(2); where all relevant facts were known when repayments were made, the two-year period under section 78A(2) expired long before assessments, with section 73(6)(a) governing mistake-of-law recoveries by reference to the accounting period of payment.
legal_issues: Construction of evidence of facts in section 78A(2) VATA 1994
Whether ECJ judgment in Primback starts limitation period
Distinction between facts and legal effect of court decisions
Interaction of sections 73, 78A, and 80(4A)-(4B)
Retrospective Finance Act 1997 limitation amendments

enrichment.short_title: Bankruptcy petition upheld against securities trader
key_facts: Jonathan Anderson traded securities through KAS Bank NV from 1996 to 1997 after Adams & Neville's liquidation, leaving a debit balance on his trading account.

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid costs order restored after preliminary issue win
key_facts: Peter Stacy and Dr Player dissolved their Flimwell Bird Park partnership; dispute arose over sale of partnership property.
Stacy won a preliminary issue that solicitors lacked authority to exchange a contract in a contract race with Marshall.
Stacy's lawyers accepted about £16,000 from Mr Mauger to fund the preliminary issue while a legal aid certificate was in force.
The deputy judge refused a costs order because regulation 64 forbade third-party payments; the Court of Appeal held that was an erroneous exercise of discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to award costs of a preliminary issue won by a legally aided claimant where third-party funding breached regulation 64.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Dr Player ordered to pay Stacy's costs of the preliminary issue subject to legal aid taxation.
enrichment.ratio: A breach of regulation 64 by receiving third-party funding does not conclusively deny a successful legally aided party costs against the opponent; inter partes costs recovered under an order are paid to the Legal Services Commission under the legal aid scheme, and the normal costs-follows-event order should be made with Mauger repaid separately.
